name: PESTEL
purpose: Which macro-environmental trends and uncertainties shape the industry?

parts.label: Political
points: Government stability, taxation, welfare policies, trade regulation

parts.label: Economic
points: GDP, inflation, disposable income, interest rates, exchange rates

parts.label: Social
points: Values and culture, lifestyle, consumerism, attitudes to work and leisure

parts.label: Technological
points: Research policy, new patents and products

parts.label: Legal
points: Legislative and regulatory constraints and changes

apply: Scan: only factors that matter for THIS industry
Assess: impact and predictability (trend vs uncertainty → scenarios)
Translate: threat or opportunity – for whom?
pitfalls: Generic factors (“inflation”) without link to the industry
Forgetting to say whether a factor fosters or hinders, and for whom
example: US protectionism since 2025 · EU board gender quotas (2026) · end of zero interest rates (2022) · Gen Z drinks less alcohol · AI answers cut publishers' traffic · shorter snow seasons for ski resorts.

name: Five Forces
purpose: How attractive is the industry – where is the value and who captures it?

parts.label: Threat of substitutes
points: Similar function, different nature, from outside the industry

apply: Rate each force low/medium/high with 2–3 case facts
Identify the right buyers and suppliers (users AND corporate clients; app stores, content creators …)
pitfalls: Limits: industry level, forces interdependent and not prioritized, rigid boundaries, static
example: Vacuum cleaners (Dyson): rivalry high, entry high, substitutes moderate, suppliers high, buyers high → unattractive, yet Dyson earns high margins through differentiation.

name: Defining the industry

parts.label: Definition
points: A group of firms producing similar products and services

example: Airlines: Asia / Europe / North America; leisure / business / freight.
